PRESENTED BY PUCK
 
Axios Communicators
By Simon Hernandez-Arthur · Aug 06, 2026

👋 ¡Qué tal! I'm reporting this and next week from Guadalajara, Mexico, my hometown, where we're spending the last weeks of summer break with family and friends.

  • Shoot me a note if you'd like some recommendations on killer street food.

This edition of Axios Communicators, edited by Christine Wang and copy edited by Kathie Bozanich, is 1,969 words, a 7.5-minute read.
 
 
1 big thing: 🙌 Fans turned communicators
 
Illustration: Maura Losch/Axios

AI can generate almost anything on a screen, but it can't re-create what happens when thousands of people gather around something they genuinely care about.

Why it matters: Communicators have long managed relationships with employees, investors, regulators and the media. Now add fans to the mix.

The big picture: "Everybody is a fan of something," says communications strategist Shawn Smith.

  • Every fandom comms strategy needs to start with knowing and understanding the audience and what will resonate, she said.
  • When done successfully, Smith said fan-driven strategies can score wins across multiple stakeholders.
  • Fans amplify stories organically across social platforms. Media pick them up. Employees feel pride when they see their company show up in cultural conversations. Investors see a brand that remains relevant.

Zoom in: Some brands borrow external fandoms by offering tangible experiences that fans can amplify.

  • Etsy hopped on the fan-made merch aspect of modern followings, connecting Olivia Rodrigo with Etsy sellers for a festival collection.
  • The official collaborative line was created by fellow fans, unlike the usual mass-produced merch.
  • "We're not trying to manufacture culture," Daniel "Monty" Montalto, Etsy's VP of brand marketing, told Axios. "We're giving fans new, personal ways to participate in communities and cultural moments they already care about."

Brands can also build their own mega-fans.

  • Jeep has one of the deepest cultures among car brands, with rituals like the Jeep Wave, huge fan-organized off-roading events and, most recently, "ducking" each other.
  • "The stories they tell about where they've gone and what they've experienced in their Jeep vehicles are often more powerful than anything we could create ourselves," a Jeep spokesperson said.
  • Employees can become a company's most passionate advocates. Apple is reportedly holding an internal lottery for retail employees to staff the in-person iPhone launch event in Cupertino next month.

Zoom out: Communicators can also bridge the two strategies by leveraging existing external fandoms to grow their own brand.

  • To build its loyalty program, World of Hyatt is creating fan experiences that members can't buy on their own, from Formula 1 driver meet-and-greets to literary retreats with Reese's Book Club authors.
  • In travel, paid influencer marketing has lost touch with authenticity, says Laurie Blair, Hyatt's senior vice president of global marketing and loyalty. "Having real members and authentic experiences is so much more meaningful," Blair said.
  • The strategy creates member experiences worth sharing, turning Formula 1 fans and BookTok readers into advocates for Hyatt itself.

Reality check: Moments like these can't be owned by one function, even if the idea originates in comms.

  • Marketing might have the budget and the creative to kick off a campaign, and frontline teams might be the ones on the ground activating it.
  • "There's such a level of trust between all of our teams that allows us to be nimble and to just move when the opportunity presents itself," said Danielle Swain, general manager from Delta's global communications team.

Between the lines: Companies that invest in fandom must contribute something communities value or risk losing credibility with the audiences they hoped to engage.

  • BMW caught flak this week for the sudden appearance of a button on the dashboard display of some cars. When pressed, an ad for the latest "Spider-Man" movie plays — which, in a press release, it touted as an exclusive "special surprise."

Flashback: Long before "community building" became corporate jargon, Comic-Con, now one of the world's most recognizable fandom conventions, expanded because fans convinced others to come.

  • David Glanzer, Comic-Con International's longtime comms chief, recalled a radio host's surprise when a contest winner chose Comic-Con passes over Grateful Dead tickets in the 1990s.
  • The contest winner told the host: "You should really check it out, as it's a really cool event."
  • Hollywood was ahead of the game in recognizing the value of reaching fans directly and generating word of mouth. Glanzer recalled the original "Star Wars" was teased with production stills and concept art at Comic-Con almost a full year before it was released
  • That kind of promotional tactic was virtually unheard of back then but has become standard practice for any blockbuster today.

Yes, but: Ultimately, community needs to drive business results.

  • "Brand awareness" alone is no longer a sufficient metric. Instead, "there needs to be connectivity back to commercial business results," says Hyatt's Blair.

The bottom line: The best way to approach fans and win them over to your side? "Share, don't sell," said Glanzer.

Share this story.
 
 
2. Corporate consistency wins
 

Illustration: Eniola Odetunde/Axios
 

Three recent studies converged on two big themes for communicators: Americans are most concerned with practical, pocketbook issues and are looking for consistency from business leaders.

Why it matters: Our inboxes are flooded with industry research, but surveys conducted by three of the largest consultancies highlight specific trends of what Americans say matters.

First, Americans' biggest concerns are increasingly practical rather than political.

  • Brunswick and Echelon Insights found that the cost of living, the economy and jobs account for 41% of voters' top concerns. Burson said 81% of Americans remain deeply concerned about the cost of living and inflation.
  • Americans also ranked fair wages, data privacy and worker safety among their top expected corporate priorities, according to APCO.

Second, Americans appear increasingly skeptical of companies that react to the political moment rather than demonstrate consistency.

  • Burson found 76% lose respect for CEOs who change public positions under outside pressure. APCO's survey showed 72% respect companies that maintain their commitments despite political pressure.
  • Brunswick and Echelon Insights found 65% want businesses to stay politically neutral and focus on serving customers.

The big picture: The findings suggest Americans are asking companies to focus on the things that affect people's daily lives and to keep showing up regardless of which way the political winds are blowing.

Case in point: Costco's board defended the company's DEI policies amid activist investor pressure, noting "many of our members like to see themselves reflected in the people in our warehouses."

  • Shareholders overwhelmingly rejected the anti-DEI proposal.
  • Costco emerged from the news cycle with its reputation unscathed, ranking fifth in the Axios Harris Poll 100 reputation rankings last year and this year.
  • In contrast, Target faced a boycott after it rolled back some of its DEI policies in 2025. It slipped from 59th in the 2024 Axios Harris rankings to 71st this year.

Simon's thought bubble: As we've covered, comms leaders can't just be messengers. They need to be peers with the rest of the C-suite, and that means pushing back on operational decisions that carry real reputational risk.

Between the lines: Saying nothing isn't necessarily safer. Audiences fill the silence themselves.

  • APCO found that 27% interpret corporate silence during major events as fear of backlash, while 22% see it as a signal that the company may quietly agree with what is happening.

Reputation doesn't only erode during major crises. It can quietly disappear through unexplained decisions, inconsistent messages and missed opportunities to communicate.

  • Burson reported 48% of Americans have gradually lost confidence in a company without being able to identify a defining moment.

The fine print: Burson surveyed 1,601 U.S. adults between April 22-30.

  • Brunswick and Echelon Insights surveyed 1,001 registered voters from June 25–28.
  • APCO's survey included 1,522 U.S. adults, fielded May 19–28.

The bottom line: Communicate about the business, focus on what matters most to your customers and ground every message in your company's values.

Share this story.
 
 
3. 🐖 Reading list: The slop wars
 

Illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios
 

The fight against AI slop is heating up.

⚠️ LinkedIn is testing out a new "seems like AI slop" reporting button and has removed some of the AI writing tools built into the platform. (Engadget)

🚫 In Utah, some businesses and organizations are vowing not to use AI to create flyers and to avoid promoting events that do, Axios Salt Lake City's Erin Alberty reports. (Axios)

  • "Please hit up a local artist, or cut out magazines or we can help too," one venue posted, adding: "DIY or die baby."

📱 Snapchat announced it won't add videos entirely generated with AI to its Spotlight section. (TechCrunch)

  • The company noted, however, content enhanced or edited with Snapchat's own AI tools will continue to be eligible.

🫠 AI-generated imagery is "eroding our sense of reality" and increasing the mental load of having to assess what's on our feeds. (Wall Street Journal)

  • "If you think about the millions of years of evolution, our neural architecture wasn't designed to say, 'Is the tiger in the brush real or fake?' It's 'Tiger! Run!'," one Dartmouth professor told the Journal.
 
 

A MESSAGE FROM PUCK

New members get even more: Puck is now bundled with Air Mail, the definitive read on culture, style and scandal. Start a 14-day free trial.

 
 
4. Spotlight: Michelle Lammers of Nightwing
 

Michelle Lammers. Photo: Courtesy of Michelle Lammers
 

Michelle Lammers has spent her career at the intersection of defense, space, cyber and national security, and now serves as vice president of communications at Nightwing, a national security technology company.

Why it matters: Lammers' "anything but linear" career reflects a broader shift in the profession, as communications leaders are increasingly expected to understand business strategy just as well as storytelling.

🏃‍♂️The path here: Lammers has held roles in strategy, business development, operations, program management, capture and communications at Airbus, RTX and now Nightwing.

  • "The diversity of my background gives me a great appreciation for not only telling the story of fascinating missions but directly connecting communications goals to the business strategy," she said.

🫣 Tough lesson: You can't communicate your way out of a strategy problem.

  • "The most effective communications start long before an announcement, crisis or change in direction," Lammers said.
  • "It begins by asking questions that help think through second- and third-order effects, bringing in different perspectives, and building alignment with others."

🔎 Trendspotting: Comms leaders are increasingly expected to lead across the enterprise, not just manage reputation.

  • "The best communicators help leaders anticipate stakeholder reactions before decisions are made, not simply communicate them afterward. That really does position the function as a driver of business outcomes," she said.

🎧 Playlist: "Whenever I can, I listen to interviews with authors across a range of disciplines from psychology to technology to economics," Lammers said.

  • Recent faves include Lorraine Marchand on "The Innovation Mindset," Dr. Julia Garcia on "The Five Habits of Hope," and Amanda Ripley on conflict and productive disagreement.

☀️ Morning ritual: "I spend 5-10 minutes outside in nature listening to the world wake up since that helps me to stay grounded and intentional throughout my day," she said.

  • That's followed by coffee, scanning the news and writing down three priorities for the workday.

🤝 Best advice: Stay curious.

  • "The best leaders don't assume they have all the answers. They ask thoughtful questions, listen carefully, and seek to understand why someone holds a different perspective," Lammers said.

5. 1 helpful thing: Natural disaster playbook
 

Illustration: Lindsey Bailey/Axios
 

Communicators now have a playbook for using their skills to support their communities during natural disasters.

Why it matters: Wildfires this year exceed the 10-year-average. Weather disasters in the first half of 2026 caused tens of billions of dollars in damages.

Context: After last year's wildfires in Los Angeles, communicators teamed up to form the LA Strong Comms Coalition to use their networks and skills to support small businesses.

  • The coalition secured media interviews for business owners whose businesses were destroyed by the fires and offered support with longer-term planning.

What they're saying: "Our hope is that by sharing what we've learned, others can leverage their communications expertise to confidently guide their own communities through recovery," said Jennifer Stephens Acree, founder and CEO of JSA+Partners, who spearheaded the initiative.

item.title: 🤖 AI perception gap
item.description:
Plus: ✍️ Claude's watermarks | Thursday, August 13, 2026
 
View in browser
 
 
Axios Communicators
By Simon Hernandez-Arthur · Aug 13, 2026

👋 Hello, communicators!

Situational awareness: Former Brunswick partner and Pinterest head of comms Christine Schirmer has joined DoorDash as vice president for global external communications, Axios exclusively reports. Go deeper.

This edition of Axios Communicators, edited by Christine Wang and copy edited by Jay Bennett is 1,912 words, a 7-minute read.
 
 
1 big thing: The AI perception bubble
 

Illustration: Allie Carl/Axios
 

AI has become an everyday tool for communicators, but many of the audiences they're trying to reach remain deeply skeptical of how it's being used.

Why it matters: Communicators risk getting stuck in a pro-AI bubble, where the ubiquity of the technology among colleagues and executives makes it easy to overlook the skepticism — and sometimes outright hostility — it generates.

  • Half of U.S. consumers prefer to give their business to brands that don't use generative AI in consumer-facing messages, advertising and content, according to a Gartner survey from earlier this year.
  • Younger consumers were particularly skeptical: 57% of Gen Z and millennials said generative AI has made content quality worse.
  • In contrast, AI has become deeply embedded in comms. Earlier this year, Muck Rack found 80% of PR professionals say they already use generative AI in their workflow.

Zoom in: Comms teams have to know the audience. That includes creators, whose livelihoods depend on understanding what their audiences will tolerate, celebrate or reject.

  • YouTuber Hank Green faced backlash after viewers of a July 29 video zeroed in on language they associated with ChatGPT and accused him of using AI to write his script.
  • Green denied the allegations but acknowledged that he'd become overly reliant on the technology for research and later shared a personal AI policy restricting how he'll use it going forward.
  • OpenAI's first influencer brand trip — a luxury "Summer Club" retreat in New York's Hudson Valley — backfired as participating creators were criticized for promoting the company amid broader concerns about AI's environmental impact, job displacement and corporate power.

The big picture: The episodes highlight just how unsettled the boundaries around acceptable AI use remain.

  • "Where do you draw the line of what's immoral and what is moral?" content creator and marketing strategist Sam Ogborn says. "It's a very subjective question that I believe every person has to answer for themselves."
  • Communicators must help companies read the room. "Don't become so fascinated with the technology that you forget your audience is human," Reddit chief communications officer Adam Collins said.
  • "The best way for communicators to avoid an AI bubble is the same way communicators have always avoided any information bubbles: Listen to people outside of it," he said.

AI companies can avoid that whiplash by figuring out where an audience's line is before crossing it.

  • "We don't want to rage bait people for no reason," says Higgsfield founding growth lead Alisher Shariyazdanov.
  • He explained the AI video company proactively addresses concerns. For example, a 10-person team studies the audiences of creators Higgsfield partners with and develops a different brief for each community of filmmakers, marketers and content creators.
  • The company also built an internal dashboard that tracks social trends to gauge the backlash risk of potential campaigns.

Zoom out: It's not just AI. There's a broadening influencer fatigue. (See the viral "no influencers" sign in Nantucket.)

  • Consumers know they're addicted to their phones and are trying to solve for that, fueling interest in tech like Brick, which locks users out of their social apps.
  • The economic backdrop and wealth gap have also left audiences irritated rather than inspired by displays of wealth, including flashy brand trips.

Between the lines: Anti-AI sentiment is part of broader anxiety about jobs, creative work, the environment and the power of technology companies.

  • Sen. Bernie Sanders on Monday called for a pause on the development of more advanced AI systems, arguing that companies are moving forward without adequately accounting for their effects on workers and society.
  • Silicon Valley's futurist predictions have fallen flat before, argue anti-AI activists.
  • Tech companies, most notably Meta, spent billions trying to build a metaverse where users could shop, go to concerts and attend meetings. And of course, who can forget NFTs?

Reality check: AI isn't like any of those things. Hundreds of millions of people already use AI products, and the technology is increasingly embedded across the economy.

  • "It's very easy to say, 'I'm anti-AI,' without recognizing that AI is embedded now in every part of our lives," said Ogborn.
  • But widespread adoption doesn't mean widespread acceptance.
  • Social media can push people to further extremes. "The more anti-AI someone becomes, the more they're going to continue to see that content," she noted.

The bottom line: The biggest risk can come from trying to appease everyone. Pick a side and be transparent with your audience, says Ogborn. "The worst is when people try to play both sides, whether it's companies or creators."

Madison Mills contributed reporting.
 
 
2. 💻 Anthropic's text watermarks signal new front in AI detection
 

Illustration: Natalie Peeples/Axios
 

Anthropic's new models will add machine-readable "watermarks" to Claude-generated text and files to comply with new European Union transparency regulations.

Why it matters: Comms teams using Claude to simply clean up, translate or format human-drafted press releases could stamp those documents with an AI signature.

How it works: For models launched in the EU after Aug. 2, Anthropic is marking content in two ways "wherever Claude is offered, worldwide."

  • Text watermarks: Claude embeds patterns into the generated text that Anthropic claims are "imperceptible."
  • File metadata: Generated media files carry digital signatures confirming the asset was processed by Claude.

Yes, but: Anthropic highlighted two major limitations to its detection tech.

  • AI-assisted can appear AI-generated: Content may trigger a detected mark even if Claude was used solely to proofread, format or translate human-written copy.
  • Detection drop-off: If text is heavily rewritten, mixed with other copy or too short, then the watermarks might not be detectable.

Zoom out: Anthropic explained its changes are designed to meet Article 50 of the EU AI Act, which mandates AI disclosures for generated or manipulated content.

  • OpenAI similarly outlined its compliance approach, though its current watermarking efforts primarily focus on images and audio rather than text.
  • The moves mark a regulatory-driven turn in the ongoing effort to help audiences identify AI-generated text, audio and visual content.
  • Digital platforms have recently accelerated their own AI identification measures: LinkedIn is testing a "seems like AI slop" button, Substack embedded Pangram's AI detection suite, and Snap stopped promoting AI-generated video in its main feed.

What's next: AI providers have until Dec. 2 to bring legacy models into compliance with EU rules, meaning we'll get a clearer picture in the coming months of how the industry's biggest players plan to mark AI-generated content.

Share this story
 
 
3. 🔦 Communicators spotlight: Jessica Kleiman from Lennar
 

Photo: Courtesy of Jessica Kleiman
 

Jessica Kleiman took a "very jagged" path from aspiring magazine writer to communications leader, with stops across media, entertainment and technology before making the jump to homebuilding.

The latest: Today, Kleiman is senior vice president of communications at Lennar, one of the nation's largest homebuilders.

The path here: Kleiman originally planned to become a writer, interning and freelancing for national magazines while in college.

  • She joined a small New York PR agency representing magazines, figuring the connections might eventually help her move into editorial.
  • Instead, "I ended up loving the PR side and the rest is history," she said.
  • Kleiman went on to spend much of her communications career in media, entertainment and technology, including four years as Peloton's first head of communications, before making "a pretty big pivot" into homebuilding.

Tough lesson: Even if you love what you do, "at the end of the day, it's just a job."

  • After leaving Peloton, "I felt like I lost an appendage because it was such a big part of my life both personally and professionally," she said. "I had to sort of 'deprogram' myself, and that took a while."

Trendspotting: The line between communications and HR is blurring as comms teams take on more responsibility for how companies engage employees and attract talent.

  • Lennar's latest employer brand campaign was a collaboration between comms, talent acquisition and early careers, with Kleiman's team spearheading the effort and owning social execution.
  • "Ten years ago that kind of campaign would have sat entirely with HR or talent acquisition," she said. "Now comms is a lead partner, because the story of why people want to work somewhere has become as important as the story of what the company builds or sells."

Currently consuming: Walter Isaacson's Steve Jobs biography ("Better late than never!")

  • Plus, a rewatch of "Arrested Development;" the "SmartLess" podcast; and Suzy Welch's "Becoming You."

Morning ritual: Nespresso with the New York Times and New York Post, followed by a few Duolingo Spanish lessons while walking her dog.

  • Fun fact: She's currently on a 589-day streak.

Best advice: Know your non-negotiables.

  • Kleiman encourages younger professionals to write down what they need from a job to be happy.
  • "You may not get every one in every role, but if you're in a job that doesn't check any of your boxes, then you know you're in the wrong place."

  • She defended the White House through multiple controversies and the biggest stories of the president's second term so far, including the Signalgate scandal, the release of the Epstein files and the Iran war.

  • Hong faced backlash over years-old social media posts, like one calling to "cancel Thanksgiving." While she later backtracked on those statements, her meandering responses didn't shake the scrutiny.
  • Without major endorsements from progressive heavyweights in the chaotic primary, the comments proved distracting and costly.

  • Ellison's New York Times op-ed last week argued efforts to block the Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery deal are political and driven by fear over his potential stewardship of CNN.
  • Bonta chose Hollywood trade Deadline for his response, defending the 12-state lawsuit against the takeover as a straightforward antitrust case.

🤖 The New York Post launched Hamilton, a Google Cloud-powered AI news assistant that uses the paper's journalism to give readers conversational search and personalized news experiences. (Axios)

  • Simon's thought bubble: Imagine all the work it takes to get your CEO quoted in a story — only for the publisher's own AI bot to summarize it without the quote! Maddening.
 
 
5. ⏭ Looking ahead: AI-powered crash courses
 

Illustration: Allie Carl/Axios
 

This earnings season I've been playing around with Google Finance's Gemini integration, which allows users to get breakdowns and analyses based on massive troves of financial data, including earnings reports and call transcripts.

  • I asked Gemini to explain some of the weedier aspects of PayPal's business — the stuff that took me a while to wrap my head around when I first joined— and I was pleasantly surprised by how well it explained things!

The big picture: As communicators are urged to become multidisciplinary operators, versed in everything from government relations to HR policies, AI-powered crash courses can help fill in knowledge gaps.
